Arca CIO Jeff Dorman says no chain can quantify its revenue strategy: when do the fees turn on, and who pays them?

"That strategy makes all the sense in the world. But again, it comes back to, if that is the strategy, why can't anybody quantify that, right?"

"Visionaries who actually believed in Facebook, the stock, said, 'Well, that's short-sighted. They're just trying to grow the biggest network in the world, and then eventually they'll turn on the fees.' Well, there were a lot of analysts back then who were quantifying that."

"Eventually it comes back to, if you actually grow that network to a size that matters, then you start collecting fees from the people using it."

"When you invested in Facebook or Google or other companies before they had a lot of revenue turned on, it wasn't like you couldn't see the vision. Some people believed, some people didn't, but you could at least quantify."

"How big does your network have to get before you start turning on fees and revenues? Who are you going to get those fees and revenues from? If you give me an answer, I might be the first investor. But nobody can do it."

The bottleneck for software engineering keeps changing.

Historically, it was writing the code and tests to ensure they conformed with the specs.

In early days of agentic coding it was reviewing code for correctness.

Now (for complex projects) it's the build & test phase.

It's rather frustrating when you can make significant code changes in 10 minutes but then it takes an hour or more to find out if it passes QA.

The most interesting lesson Jensen Huang taught me

And gave PTSD to Google executives over from his leadership at $NVDA:

Was that if a critical material can be bought out for spare change eg. ~$400m (FY2028 Photonics-SOI revenue forecast for $SOI)

And trigger tens of billions in economic impact to competitors for not securing supply:

We're going to see game theory bottleneck supply procurement actually accelerate upstream through 2027, with or without him. 

I see Morgan Stanley's list highlighting CCL, ABF, PCBs, optical module components as interesting. 

However; I'd put it through my own narrower lens, especially focusing on smaller component cost chokepoints + bottlenecks that doesn't cost much to secure capacity over. 

Deleveraging/negative sentiment is indiscriminately moving the theme up and down together, so hard to argue individual fundamentals at this point. 

Reflecting on 2026, I also prob need to be more selective of companies entering 2027:

But there's going to be a lot of outsized opportunities in bottlenecks... as new architectures like NPO/CPO emerge across the ecosystem.

There’s a growing narrative that $NVDA has downside because $MU trades at 4x CY27 earnings vs 10x for NVIDIA.

Both are hardware companies that have surged on AI infrastructure spending.

But this view misses two key points:

1. Upcoming growth: Street expects Micron’s earnings to grow 18% in CY27 vs 68% for Nvidia. Even if Micron reaches 30% growth and tighter Asia restrictions slow Nvidia to 45%, Nvidia would still be growing 50% faster.

2. The businesses are fundamentally different: Micron operates largely in a cyclical, commodity memory market, while Nvidia’s proprietary GPUs and CUDA software create stronger competitive moat.

David Sacks: Who Risked Jail to Take Down Jensen Huang?

“I think it's pretty clear that there were two ops here.

So one op is whatever Alice Huang was doing with or without the Chinese Communist Party. There may have been smuggling involved, we don't know. There is an investigation going on, and there should be an investigation. We should get all the facts there.

However, there's also a second op here. That second op began when somebody, or multiple people, leaked a highly classified memo, or the contents of it, to The New York Times. I think it's really important to understand that that's a crime. Leaking classified intelligence is a crime, and many people have been prosecuted for it.

Because of that fact, I don't believe that The New York Times just got this by overhearing people talking about it at a bar. Somebody made the calculated decision that they're willing to risk going to jail, they're willing to risk committing a crime to let The New York Times know about this story.

I have a series of questions about that.

So number one is, first, who did that and why? What was their motivation? Why did they feel so strongly about taking Jensen down?

Bucket number two is around the failure to give the defensive briefing. If the national security state is worried that Jensen is in possession of national security secrets and might leak them to someone who they suspect is a spy, why wouldn't you go to him right away and tell him, ‘Hey, you have this problem. Don't talk to this person’? Apparently, that didn't happen, and it does sound like that is some sort of standard operating procedure.

That brings me to question number three, which is what exactly were the national security secrets that Jensen supposedly knew? He doesn't work for the government. He's not, as far as I'm aware, privy to classified materials. So what is it that people say that he leaked to this suspected intelligence asset?

The last question I have is, what is the evidence that this person, Alice Huang, was actually a Chinese spy who worked for the Ministry of State Security? Just this morning, the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, who's a Democrat, came out of a classified briefing on this subject and said that he's not sure that this person is a Chinese spy.

So I put all these things together and I would say, at this point in time, I think there's more questions than answers. And I would like a full accounting of the facts to come out.”
